title: The Huntress
mood: The pull has a direction now. Selena hunts it, faces a dark window, and leaves Karina’s door at dawn.

hero.alt: Framed in a pane of pale glass against the dark, Selena in her school uniform touches her fingers to her chin and smiles at her own reflection.

segs.t: Rain hammered the broken wall in the outskirts. Selena sat astride Silverbolt with both palms on its back and her phone in the socket under the seat.
The report was already sent.

Now she waited for the slack. After every report the pull in her cells had sunk to a murmur for a while. Then a place would come into her head, a ditch with a downed Ender in it, and by nightfall the plates were sold.
Tonight the pull grew harder while she sat there.
“Well?” she asked the dark.
The next morning, at the sink, her head stayed empty. The morning after, the same.
In the next storm she sent another. Nothing came back.
After that the pull was stronger every night, and nearer. Some nights it kept her awake until the windows went gray.
So much for the market,
she thought.
Whoever’s at the other end doesn’t need to bargain anymore.
She did not send again.
When the rain came again, she went hunting instead.
Her own thread had never told her where it ended. The pull was another thing. It had a direction.

On the bell tower she laid her palms on Silverbolt’s back and let the purple into its core. The pull ran through her and through the Ender plates. She let it run and read it, the way she read a dead arm on Chang’e’s bench: fingers on the casing, feeling where the current went.
Over the bay. She drew the line on her phone’s map with her thumb.
Then she rode to a roof at the far end of the outskirts, where the lit streets gave out, and read it again.
Anything far off would have pointed the same way from both roofs. This one slanted.
“Oh?” said Selena.
Her two lines crossed on the water past the dome’s seaward edge, where the faint point hung. Rain hid it tonight. She knew where it was.
She followed the pull out past the crossing. At the point it kept going, like a wire through a hole in a wall, on into whatever lay behind the sky.
She had never seen her maker, but she had never doubted there was one. Somebody had made the hum in her bones.
A hunter,
she thought. Then, without knowing why she was sure:
A huntress.
For weeks she had felt it without a word for it. The fearsome huntress was already crossing the sea of stars, closing in on Selena.
Now the crossing was over. The huntress was waiting right behind the Singularity.
Back on the bell tower she sat on the wet tiles with Silverbolt crouched against her, its plates steaming in the rain. Below her the city’s lamps burned, street after street, down to the water.
Nobody travels that far for one runaway alone,
she thought.
Whatever comes through that point is coming for the whole city.
Once Selena realized someone from the Mother Matrix was coming for her, she quickly weighed the choice that best served her survival and interests.
She laid the roads out in her head the way she sorted plates under the workshop lamp. Whole ones for sale. Cracked ones for the bin.
She had no intention of returning to a Mother Matrix ruled by nothing but slaughter and control.
Bin.
Nor did she intend to die protecting humanity.
Bin.
Saying no to going back had a price. Nobody had taught her the rule. Her body knew it anyway. A pawn could run loose for a while. If it ever got away for good, it was finished.
One road she turned over twice. Whoever sat at the far end of the pull gave the orders. Whoever gave the orders had a seat. If it came to that, she could take the huntress’s own seat.
Selena smiled into the rain. Then she set that one aside.
Later,
she thought. She had decided nothing.
“If it’s all going to end anyway, we’d better enjoy the show to the fullest.” Selena patted Silverbolt’s neck.
Long past midnight she went down through the Science Division. The workshop was empty. The lamp over the long bench was off, and the windows were black glass.
In one of them a girl in a wet uniform stopped and looked back.
Let’s see what the huntress is coming for,
Selena thought.
When she was small, she had practiced smiles in dark glass like this. One borrowed face at a time.
Tonight she let the purple up, on the left side only. It climbed her arm and her collarbone, then the side of her throat to the cheek. Pale plates rose through it at the wrist and the shoulder.
In the glass the right half was the Academy’s Selena, the one in every class photo. The left half was the Ender.
She tilted her head. Both halves tilted with her.
She touched her right cheek, the human one.
The huntress made this face too.
“Fate, huh. Don’t you think it’d be more fun to smash it to smithereens?” she asked the girl in the glass.
Then she let it all go back down until the glass showed only a schoolgirl, and walked home through the last of the rain.
Karina’s flat. The day before.
At first light Selena sat by the door, lacing her boots. Nobody had called her yet. In all her years in the flat, she had never once been up first.
She had hardly slept in the days since the storm.
On the shelf the team radio talked low.
“Cliff watch doubled through tonight,” it said. “Point over the bay, no change. All teams on standby.”
Not that you can see from here,
Selena thought.
Karina stood by the shelf in her boots and coat, her helmet under her arm, and listened to the end. Then she turned it down.
“Standby?” asked Selena.
“All of us.”
Karina came to the door. Every morning, about now, she said, “The bell.”
She did not say it. She leaned in the open door to the stair and waited while Selena tied the second lace.
Selena stood up. Karina stayed in the doorway.

Karina reached into her coat, into the pocket she had mended at the table years ago. It was the pocket where she kept sweets for the children she carried out. She took out a fruit drop in a twist of paper and pressed it into Selena’s palm.
“I’ve noticed things,” said Karina. “I never asked. I’m not asking now.”
Selena’s mind went down the list before she could stop it.
Hands warm after every storm. A whole winter without one cold. The bed still made at dawn. A fever phoned in for a girl who never had one.
She kept count,
thought Selena.
All of it.
You don’t put down someone you carried out.
Karina had told the clerk that over the shelter’s log, the second night. Selena had kept those words too.
So she never asked,
Selena thought.
If she asked, she’d know, and then she might have to put me down.
The radio hissed a street name. Karina did not look at it. She looked at Selena the way she had over the lamp in the rain, that first night.
“Come home after,” said Karina.
Selena’s face did not change.
But her free hand had closed in the hem of Karina’s coat. She did not remember doing it.
Everything in this city has a price,
she thought.
So what’s hers?
She went through it twice. Years of covering, and Karina had never named a price. The sum would not come out.
“I still want to see you graduate,” said Karina.
Selena opened her fingers one at a time and let the coat go.
Karina stepped out of the doorway. She did not tell her to hurry.
Selena went down the stair. All the way down she listened for the door. It did not close.
At the bottom Silverbolt unfolded from the wall.
The fruit drop was still in her fist. Since the first one in the shelter, she had let every sweet melt slowly to nothing. This one she put in her pocket, still wrapped.
In her cells the pull tugged toward the water.
Everybody wants me home today,
she thought.
Over the bay the faint point hung in the gray morning. She thought it was brighter than yesterday.
She did not look at it long.
